Beállítom Orosz támadás érte Harkiv egyik lakótelepét vasárnap reggel. Ukrajna második legnagyobb városának polgármestere számolt be arról, hogy előbb az egyik lakóház hetedik és tizedik szintje között volt becsapódás , majd a szomszédos épületet is találat érte Szaltyivka városrészben, amely az Oroszország által Ukrajna ellen 2022 februárjában indított háborúban már az első óráktól célpont volt és azóta is számos találat érte. A vasárnapi támadásban két ember meghalt, tucatnyian megsebesültek, és a beszámolók szerint a romok alatt túlélők is vannak, akiknek kimentése a reggeli órákban folyamatban van – írta az Ukrainszka Pravda. Eközben a békeidőben 1,4 milliós Harkivtól 600 kilométerre, az ország másik milliós városát, Odesszát is találatok érték vasárnapra virradó éjszaka. Halálos áldozatok nincsenek, de több helyen akadozik az áram- és a vízellátás. A támadást ballisztikus rakétákkal hajtották végre az orosz erők. Ezek ellen az ukrán légvédelem az utóbbi időben kevéssé hatákony, Ukrajna már többször jelezte nyugati partnereinekhogy sürgősen szükságe lenne Patriot-rakétákra és további légvédelmi rakétarendszerekre a védelem megerősítése érdekében. Az Egyesült Államok elnöke korábban ígéretet adott, hogy a Patriot-rakéták gyártási licenszét is kész átadni Ukrajnának, Donald Trump azonban július végén visszakozott az ígérettől. A kész rakéták leszállítását pedig akadályozza az, hogy az Egyesült Államok az Irán elleni katonai akciók során maga is épít saját készleteire, így – noha az EU és külön több európai ország finanszírozza az Ukrajnának szánt amerikai fegyvereket –, Kijev jelenleg kevésbé számíthat ezekre a szállítmányokra. http://www.bignewsnetwork.com/news/27935.text: Big News Network.com 'Everyone knows' Kiev is embezzling Western aid - ex-Polish PM Leszek Miller has called for suspending assistance to Ukraine until it accounts for previously supplied weaponry and funds Ukrainian officials are embezzling foreign financial aid, former Polish Prime Minister Leszek Miller has said, adding that Kiev's backers are well aware of the corruption but prefer not to ask questions. Speaking on the 'Jankowski Kontra' podcast on Polsat News on Saturday, Miller called for suspending aid to Ukraine until Kiev accounts for previously supplied weapons and funds. "Nobody's asking what happened to the 300 tanks we sent in the first phase. What happened to the heavy equipment, the lighter equipment... Nobody's asking what happened to the billions of euros we donated. Mr. Zelensky simply comes and says, 'Give it', and we give it," Miller stated. Asked whether he suspected that funds transferred to Ukraine were being embezzled, Miller replied: "Of course, everyone knows it." The veteran politician argued that Warsaw should demand an accounting of how its assistance has been used and halt further support if Kiev fails to provide one. "This is a fundamental issue: I'll lend you the money, but give me a report on what you did with the previous installment," Miller stated. "Without that help, there is no Ukraine... But we are not a country that is overflowing with wealth... We have obligations to our own citizens, and we cannot simply throw away money and equipment indiscriminately." Poland has been one of Kiev's staunchest backers in its conflict with Russia, pouring billions into military, financial and humanitarian aid while serving as a crucial hub for Western supplies. Yet relations have increasingly soured over Kiev's honoring of Ukrainian Nazi collaborators linked to the World War II-era Volhynia massacres, in which UPA militants, linked to the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN), killed at least 100,000 ethnic Poles. Warsaw recognizes the killings as genocide, while Kiev honors figures including OUN leader Stepan Bandera. Tensions flared again this year after Zelensky bestowed the title 'Heroes of the UPA' on the Ukrainian Special Operations Center North military unit. In the aftermath, Polish President Karol Nawrocki stripped him of the country's highest honor, politicians on both sides renounced state decorations, and Warsaw threatened to obstruct Ukraine's EU accession. Relations have also been strained by mounting opposition to Ukrainian refugees. A July CBOS survey found that 52% of Poles now opposed accepting them, against 42% in favor - a sharp reversal from the overwhelming support seen after Kiev's conflict with Moscow escalated in 2022. Tensions deepened earlier this month after a 31-year-old Ukrainian man stabbed five people at a Benedictine abbey in Jaroslaw, killing a priest. Poland is also not alone in questioning funding for Kiev. Despite receiving billions in Western assistance over the past four years, Ukraine faces a severe cash squeeze and has been pressing European backers for more money. But a string of high-level graft scandals has heightened scrutiny in Brussels, the largest of which centers on an alleged $100 million kickback scheme at state nuclear operator Energoatom, which was reportedly led by Timur Mindich, a former business partner of Vladimir Zelensky. Western-backed investigators have uncovered multiple other graft schemes involving Ukrainian officials, including one reported earlier this month in which they allegedly embezzled more than $3 million through the delivery of used Soviet-made metro cars donated by Poland. Against that backdrop, the EU this week rebuffed Kiev's bid to fast-track its latest 90 billion support loan, making clear that further funds depend on Ukraine delivering promised anti-corruption and governance reforms. Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP View image in fullscreen Greens leader, David Shoebridge, said ‘the ombudsman has told us now that this [algorithm tool] has been unfair from the moment it was conceived of’. Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP Aged care Greens push for human override in aged care assessment after ombudsman’s scathing report into algorithm tool Investigation recommends government changes legislation so staff assessing people for home support packages can correct the outcome Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Melissa Davey Medical editor Tue 27 Oct 2026 10.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 10.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Greens leader, David Shoebridge , has used a scathing report from the commonwealth ombudsman to press the government to use the last two sitting weeks of parliament to restore human override to its “unfair” aged care assessment tool. The 104-page ombudsman report , published on Monday, recommends the government change legislation so that aged care workers assessing older Australians for home support packages can amend the outcome when the algorithm-driven assessment tool makes an incorrect decision on funding. Known as the Integrated Assessment Tool (IAT), the ombudsman found it is leading to unfair outcomes, and has undermined the public’s confidence in aged care. Assessors meet older people, complete a questionnaire about their needs, and an algorithm then decides whether funding should be allocated, and at what level. “People are tearing their hair out at what’s happening,” Shoebridge said. Health officials in turmoil over 11th-hour backflip on aged care algorithm override powers, emails reveal Read more “We’ve got aged care workers who are trying to help their clients … and the computer just says no. The ombudsman has told us now that this has been unfair from the moment it was conceived of. That it’s producing arbitrary and unfair outcomes for people who are at a stage of life where they desperately need help and support.” State health officials were so alarmed by algorithmic changes to the IAT, introduced in November, that they kept a log of hundreds of cases where vulnerable older Australians were severely under-assessed, Guardian Australia previously revealed. In a joint statement, the aged care minister, Sam Rae, and the health minister, Mark Butler, said the government will “consider the Ombudsman’s report carefully” and are acting on some of its recommendations. The government has commissioned an independent review of how the IAT assesses and prioritises people. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here Of the 10 recommendations made, six were accepted and two, including instating human override for assessors and amending the aged care legislation, were noted. “We have two more sitting weeks of parliament, where the Senate and the House of Reps can come to some arrangement and put in place a human override for aged care,” Shoebridge said. Rae said that a new escalation pathway had already been introduced, allowing a wrong outcome to be escalated for review by a delegate, “adding a further layer of human oversight and nuance to the assessment system”. “Our response aligns with the principles of the ombudsman’s report, allowing for human discretion to overturn assessment decisions that are not fit for purpose in a way that is fair and responsible for all older people.” The commonwealth ombudsman, Iain Anderson, said: “I think that assessors being able to change decisions because they appear to be clinically inappropriate is really important, and so I am concerned that the escalation pathway will not necessarily do that”. An aged care assessor with more than four decades of nursing experience, who spoke to Guardian Australia on condition of anonymity, said escalation pathways are not good enough. “The delegate has not sat in front of that older person,” she said. “The delegate has not laid eyes on that person. I have.” She said while she escalates cases to a delegate in her workplace, who received special training to review cases, this adds time and administrative work. ‘Catastrophic’ fears: health staff made lists of concerning cases days after Australia’s aged care funding tool launch Read more She said she and her colleagues are experiencing severe anxiety and distress due to their work. “I’m too scared to ‘accept’ on the algorithm’s decision, but I have no choice,” she said. “It feels like I’m telling the algorithm and the government, ‘great choice’ and sometimes I need to walk away from the computer because I can’t hit the button. “It’s not Sam Rae or Mark Butler that then has to face the client. They’re not standing there after spending hours with clients, some of them in tears, and then telling them what the outcome is. I want the ministers to come to work with me and see what is happening.” She said she has become “so anxious, and I get so agonised over every question that I ask my clients, that it puts me into a situation where I’m not finishing my work on time, I’m not reaching my KPIs, I’m working weeknights and weekends, and I am considering leaving this job.” The shadow aged care minister, Anne Ruston, told the ABC’s Radio National on Tuesday that “the government needs to actually put proper human override back in,” describing the escalation pathway as “only a Band-Aid on a symptom”. Independent senator David Pocock accused the government of “resisting attempts to fix a problem it created”. “The Senate has offered a solution , the Ombudsman has now backed it, and the government needs to explain why it’s still standing in the way,” he said. “The Ombudsman’s findings are extraordinary, including a finding that the department responsible for designing this system didn’t even understand the legal framework it had created.” Explore more on these topics Aged care Health Australian politics David Shoebridge Australian Greens news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Guardian Essential poll: One Nation and Labor’s primary vote on par as discontent with Albanese rises If the Albanese government wants to cheat the populist death spiral, it needs to go to the barricades with the rest of us Unreasonable and unfair: damning investigation criticises Labor’s algorithm-based tool for aged care What happens to a dog when its owner can’t leave hospital? ‘Catastrophic’ fears: health staff made lists of concerning cases days after Australia’s aged care funding tool launch MP calls for rethink of pre-poll voting amid heightened security concerns in wake of Haines incident Albanese concedes $6m golf club grant in his electorate was not to contain ‘raw sewage’ A $1.95m deposit and $10k a month: welcome to the for-profit world of Australian aged care where no one is a winner ‘Are you waiting for me to be attacked?’ Fatima Payman slams PM over staffing A fifth of older Australians who contested automated decision on home support funding got more after human review Most viewed Most viewed Australia World AU politics Environment Climate crisis Indigenous Australia Immigration Media Business Health Science Tech Podcasts Newsletters
